threads.body: This `typeMatcher` includes `MultiKeyPipelineBase`, and the `QueueCommandAdvice` is applied to every public method returning `Response`. In Jedis 3.x, `Transaction` also extends `MultiKeyPipelineBase` and inherits those `Response`-returning command methods from the base classes, so issuing commands inside a `MULTI`/`EXEC` transaction will call `JedisPipelineContext.enter(...)` and have each command captured by `JedisPipelineContext.capture(...)` — which suppresses the per-command span. However, `Transaction` is completed via `exec()`/`discard()`, not `sync()`/`syncAndReturnAll()`, so the `SyncAdvice` never fires and no aggregated batch span is ever produced. The net effect is that transaction command spans, which were previously emitted by the `Connection.sendCommand` instrumentation, would be silently dropped. Please verify the transaction path; the `jedis-2.0` and `jedis-4.0` modules use the same capture approach and should be checked as well (note `jedis-2.0` casts to `Pipeline`, which behaves differently for `Transaction`).

replies.body:
Good catch — fixed in https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/commit/b2a0061374fa87c2ddb6a6f1662fefc57ef268b0.

Verified all three modules:
- **jedis-3.0**: real bug. The context casts to `PipelineBase`, and a 3.x `Transaction` is a `PipelineBase`, so its commands were captured but never flushed (no `sync()`), dropping the spans. Now `enter()` is gated on `pipeline instanceof Pipeline`, so transaction commands keep their per-command spans.
- **jedis-2.0**: was functional but only because the `(Pipeline)` cast in `enter()` threw a `ClassCastException` that `suppress = Throwable.class` swallowed on every transaction command. Added the same `instanceof Pipeline` guard so it no longer relies on a thrown/suppressed exception.
- **jedis-4.0**: unaffected — its matcher only targets `Pipeline`/`PipelineBase` and instruments `appendCommand`; a 4.x `Transaction` (extends `TransactionBase`) is never matched.

replies.body: `Object` is necessary here. In jedis 2.x the `Response`-returning queue methods are declared on `PipelineBase`, so `QueueCommandAdvice` is woven into `PipelineBase` — which is not assignable to `Pipeline`, and isn't even on the compile classpath (the module's `library("redis.clients:jedis:2.0.0")` floor only has `Pipeline`). So `@Advice.This` has to be a supertype of both `Pipeline` (2.0.0) and `PipelineBase` (2.1+), i.e. `Object`; the `instanceof Pipeline` guard in `enter(...)` does the runtime narrowing. (4.0 can use `Pipeline` because `appendCommand` is declared on `Pipeline` itself; 3.0 can use `PipelineBase` since it compiles against 3.x.)

This was a real regression fixed during review, yet there is no test exercising the transaction path. Consider adding a regression test that issues commands inside a `multi()`/`exec()` transaction and asserts the per-command spans are still emitted, so a future refactor can't reintroduce the dropped-span bug. The same gap applies to the `jedis-2.0` module's equivalent guard.

replies.body: The transaction path is now covered: jedis-2.0/3.0/4.0 each have a parameterized `transactionCommand` test that issues commands inside `multi()`/`exec()`. Note the behavior intentionally changed in this PR — per the Redis semconv, a transaction is now emitted as a single `MULTI` / `MULTI <CMD>` batch span (symmetric to pipeline `PIPELINE` batching) rather than per-command spans. The guard no longer excludes `Transaction`; transaction commands are captured and flushed as the batch span at `exec()` (dropped on `discard()`), which also removes the original dropped-span risk (fa5ea6c1bf).

threads.body: The batch query-text builder here caps the concatenated text at a 32 KB `LIMIT` and stops appending once the limit would be exceeded, but the equivalent `pipelineQueryText` added in the `jedis-3.0` and `jedis-4.0` modules uses an unbounded `StringJoiner` with no limit at all. As a result, a large pipeline/transaction produces a truncated `db.query.text` in the 2.0 module but an unbounded one in 3.0/4.0. In addition, when truncation does occur here, `db.operation.batch.size` (set from `requests.size()` in `createBatch`) still reflects the full command count, so the two attributes disagree about how many commands the batch contains. Consider aligning the three implementations — apply the same bound (and ideally the same `StringJoiner`-style code) in all modules, or drop it from this one — so the behavior is consistent across versions.
